description:
We are a multidisciplinary Peruvian team of students from software, cybersecurity, computer and environmental engineers working to address and raise awareness about wildfires around the world for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Software builds the tools, cybersecurity keeps them safe, computer engineering makes them run, and environmental engineering makes sure they matter.
summary:
Hanaq is the Quechua word for "above": the sky, the upper world of Andean tradition. That is where the satellites are. McHanaq, our team name Los McLovin joined to Hanaq, puts what they see in order.
McHanaq is a web application that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS and VIIRS into one burning activity calendar for Peru: 196 provinces and 231 hydrographic units. That record is split across sensors whose counts cannot be added, so McHanaq never adds them. It puts MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua and VIIRS S-NPP through the same rules: the same territories, the same months, a rate normalized by the pixels each sensor resolves, and an anomaly against that sensor's own history. Then it reports whether the sensors agree. A user picks a territory, reads a month-by-year heat map in a colorblind-safe ramp, sees which months and years burned most, compares the current month with the historical median, and downloads the data as CSV. This matters because MODIS is near the end of its life: a calendar that survives the handover to VIIRS keeps the long satellite fire record usable for those who plan monitoring and response.
details:
What exactly does it do?

McHanaq is a burning activity calendar for a territory you choose. You select a province or a hydrographic unit, a sensor and a date, and the app shows:

  • A month-by-year heat map of hotspot activity, in 2D or as a 3D relief where fire seasons rise as ridges.
  • The daily series for the selected month: detections, active days, the longest run of consecutive active days and how much of the territory the satellite could observe.
  • A seasonal anomaly: how this month compares with the median of the same month in earlier years, for the same sensor.
  • A side-by-side comparison of MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua and VIIRS S-NPP with a plain verdict: both elevated, both normal, in disagreement, single sensor, or not enough data.
  • A CSV download of the daily series, with every row labeled by its data origin.
  • A 7-step guided visual tour, so a first-time user can read the tool without training.

The map lets you click any polygon or draw your own area of interest; the simulation also accepts a typed latitude and longitude. Base maps switch between dark, relief and satellite.








How does it work?

We do not merge hotspot counts. MODIS and VIIRS differ in pixel size, sensitivity and overpass time, so a summed count would mean nothing. Instead, every sensor goes through the same four rules:

  1. Same definitions. Only nominal- and high-confidence detections enter the main indicator. Low-confidence detections are kept apart for sensitivity checks.
  2. Same space and time. Detections are aggregated to the same polygons (INEI provinces and ANA hydrographic units) and the same calendar months.
  3. A rate, not a count. Activity rate = fire pixel-days / valid land pixel-days. Each sensor is normalized by what it could observe. A cloudy or missing day is stored as "no observation", never as zero fire.
  4. Its own baseline. Each month is scored against the same calendar month of earlier years for that sensor, with a robust z-score (median and MAD), and only when at least five baseline years exist.

Only then are sensors compared, as signals and not as counts. A sensor is "elevated" when its own robust z-score reaches 2.0 with at least 70% observation coverage. This is the point where, in the words of the challenge, the sensor of origin no longer matters and the patterns, trends and anomalies become the focus.








The pipeline has four stages. Google Earth Engine scripts and the NASA FIRMS archive supply daily detections per territory and sensor. A Python analytics module computes rates, anomalies, sensor agreement and the rule tree, and writes precomputed JSON. A read-only FastAPI service with 10 endpoints validates and serves those files. A React and Leaflet viewer displays them. The browser never computes an indicator, and 37 automated tests check the analytics, the API contract and the acceptance criteria.








Two context layers

Contextual susceptibility. A transparent rule tree, not a trained model, describes how favorable the month's conditions are to fire spread if an ignition occurred. It asks, in order: is at least 20% of the territory burnable vegetation? Is there a dryness signal (30-day rainfall or soil moisture below the seasonal 25th percentile)? Is the wind above its seasonal 75th percentile, or is it both hot and dry? The answer is high, moderate or low, shown with its full decision path and the value, unit, source and period behind each rule. Surface water within a 150 m buffer lowers a "high" to "moderate". If a required input is missing, the result is "not evaluable" instead of a guess.

Exploratory 48-hour spread. The user places a hypothetical ignition anywhere in the world. A cellular-automaton model spreads it hour by hour using vegetation fuel from Sentinel-2 (SAVI), slope from the Copernicus DEM and hourly wind, with the elliptical fire shape of Anderson (1983) and the moisture damping of Rothermel (1972). It draws isochrones at 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 hours and exports a GIF, an MP4 and shapefiles ready for QGIS. It is labeled on screen as exploratory and unvalidated: it does not predict where or when a fire will start and is not for operational or evacuation decisions.



What makes it different

NASA FIRMS shows where fires are being detected. McHanaq shows when a territory's activity departs from its own season, and how much the satellites could see.

  • "No data" is never "no fire". Clouds and gaps appear as coverage, not as zeros. A missing value reads "no data" in the interface and stays empty in the CSV.
  • Agreement instead of a blended number. When Terra, Aqua and VIIRS disagree, the app says so instead of hiding it in an average.
  • Two lenses on the same land. Administrative provinces for decision-makers and river basins for the people who manage ecosystems. Fire does not follow political borders.
  • Explainable end to end. Every category comes with the path that produced it.
  • It states what it does not do. The landing page carries a "Does / Does not" panel: no ignition prediction, no fire probability, no claim that a hotspot is a confirmed fire, no operational alerts.
  • Accessible by design. The Cividis color ramp is readable with color-vision deficiency.

What benefits does it have?

  • Early warning and emergency teams see which months are historically critical in their territory and whether the current month is unusual, before deciding where to watch.
  • Land and basin managers compare provinces or watersheds under the same rules and separate cloudy years from quiet years.
  • Scientists get a clean daily CSV with sensors kept apart, explicit missing values and the source product on every row.

Current status and limits

A hotspot is a thermal anomaly, not a confirmed fire or a burned-area perimeter. The harmonization is semantic, temporal and statistical; it is not a radiometric calibration between instruments. The susceptibility category is qualitative and has not been validated against observed fire spread.

What do you hope to achieve?

  • Publish the full calendar for all of Peru: the geometries of 196 provinces and 231 hydrographic units are already in the application.
  • Add VIIRS on NOAA-20 as a fourth sensor, so the record continues after S-NPP.
  • Check the rule tree against mapped burned area (MODIS MCD64A1 and MapBiomas Fuego).
  • Offer the interface in English and Spanish, and test it with regional fire-monitoring staff in the Peruvian Amazon.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: Python 3.11, TypeScript and JavaScript (Earth Engine). No database: versioned JSON and GeoJSON files.
  • Geospatial processing: Google Earth Engine, GeoPandas, Shapely.
  • Analytics: pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and Pillow for the simulation exports.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx, pytest.
  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, Leaflet, Recharts.
  • Hosting: Microsoft Azure App Service, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Actions.
  • Code: https://github.com/sebastiansb1232-boop/McHanaq-labs

Team

Los McLovin, Peru. Tom: lead, analytics and integration. Angelo: NASA data, spread model and backend. Sebastian: frontend, hosting and deployment. Jean Pierrer: documentation, review and presentation.

















Target audience

Regional environmental-monitoring and emergency-planning teams, land and watershed managers, and researchers studying seasonal thermal activity across the Peruvian Amazon. McHanaq supports territorial analysis and planning; it is not an operational alert or evacuation tool.
